To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) practical and creative abilities, as assessed by our test, predict college grade-point average and business school performance beyond the predictive power of the SAT and GMAT, respectively, and (b) the test is more fair than the SAT or GMAT in predicting performance for women and minority students, and (c) our test is less biased against minority students than the SAT and GMATH, as assessed by the degree to which the test scores of minority students are more similar to those of White students

(a) the Rainbow Project tests of analytical, practical and creative skills predict performance in college better than high school grades and the SAT, and better than the SAT alone, (b) the Rainbow Project measures of analytical, practical skills, and creative skills reduce the ethnic group disparity in test scores relative to the SAT, and (c) the Michigan Business School measures of practical skills predict performance inside and outside of the classroom and explain variance in performance beyond that explained by the GMAT and undergraduate grades.
the SAT and GMAT are not the best measures of the skills and knowledge required to be successful in college and graduate school, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of theory-based university admissions testing.

developing theory based tests of abilities and skills that are relevant to the kinds of work that students will do in their careers and to the kinds of skills that students will need for successful performance.
the development of tests of practical intelligence, and the use of such tests in the prediction of performance in college.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two studies provide evidence for the validity of the theory-based tests.
theory based testing can provide more valid and equitable measures of abilities that predict academic performance than traditional testing.

theory based admissions testing has the potential to provide more valid predictions of academic performance, to reduce ethnic group disparities in admissions test scores, and to provide a more accurate and fairer picture of applicants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to move beyond the traditional view of admissions testing that focuses on analytical ability and to include a broader range of skills.
we have found that the SAT is an inadequate test of intelligence for admissions purposes, and that the GMAT is an inadequate measure of intelligence for business school admissions.
the Rainbow and Michigan projects demonstrate the potential of using tests based on Sternberg's theory to enhance the validity of university admissions testing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a broader range of cognitive abilities in admissions testing can help to reduce ethnic group disparities.
the SAT and GMAT do not provide the best measures of the skills that are most relevant to success in college and business school.
there are other ways to assess intelligence and other ways to assess performance than the traditional methods.
